name: Great Smoky Mountains
blurb: Mast-rich hardwood forests, salamanders and bears under threat from tiny pests.

tip.title: Fail the acorn crop
tip.text: Oak mast fuels bears, turkeys, deer and squirrels. Cut Oaks & hickories and see the animals that depend on autumn nuts, and the predators above them, feel it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
NPS: Mammals of Great Smoky Mountains

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Oaks & hickories
nodes.desc: Dominant trees of the drier forest. Their acorns and nuts are the fall mast that bears, turkeys, deer and squirrels fatten on.

nodes.name: American chestnut
nodes.desc: Once a major canopy tree, it was killed off by chestnut blight in the early to mid 1900s. Sprouts still grow but rarely reach the canopy.

nodes.name: Eastern hemlock
nodes.desc: A dominant cove tree that shades cool streams and damp ground. The hemlock woolly adelgid, which sucks sap from the tree, is killing hemlocks across the southern Appalachians.

nodes.name: Berries & understory plants
nodes.desc: Blueberries, huckleberries and other soft fruits and greens that feed bears, turkeys and deer in summer.

nodes.name: Fraser fir
nodes.desc: Grows near the highest summits. The balsam woolly adelgid killed most mature firs from the 1960s on, though young firs are regrowing on some peaks.

nodes.name: Leaf-litter invertebrates
nodes.desc: Tiny animals that eat decaying leaves and fungi on the forest floor. They are food for salamanders and firefly larvae.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Browses plants and eats acorns. The NPS lists bobcats and coyotes among the predators that help keep deer numbers in check.

nodes.name: Gray squirrel
nodes.desc: Eats and caches acorns and nuts. Bears are known to raid squirrel nut caches.

nodes.name: Wild turkey
nodes.desc: Forages on the forest floor for acorns, fruits and insects.

nodes.name: Elk
nodes.desc: The park's largest mammal. Overhunting removed it, and it was reintroduced in 2001, now seen mostly in Cataloochee and Oconaluftee. Grazes grass and other plants.

nodes.name: Stream insects
nodes.desc: Larvae in cold streams feed on leaf litter and algae, and in turn feed trout and stream salamanders.

nodes.name: Lungless salamanders
nodes.desc: The Smokies hold up to 31 salamander species, earning the title Salamander Capital of the World. These small amphibians eat tiny invertebrates.

nodes.name: Synchronous firefly
nodes.desc: Famous for synchronized flashing in early summer near Elkmont. Its larvae live in soil and eat snails, worms and other soft-bodied animals.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: About 1,900 bears live in the park. Mostly plant eaters, they switch from fruit in summer to hard mast in autumn, and also take insects, trout, carrion and fawns.

nodes.name: Brook trout
nodes.desc: The park's only native trout, now mostly in cold high streams after non-native rainbow and brown trout took over lower reaches. Eats insects and small animals.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: The only wild cat left in the park. Preys on deer and smaller animals such as squirrels and turkeys.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Arrived in the late 1900s and is now the park's largest wild canine, filling the role left after the failed red wolf reintroduction of 1991.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Powers the leafy summer canopy and the understory below it.

nodes.name: Rain & mountain fog
nodes.desc: Heavy rainfall and cool, moist air keep the high forests and streams wet.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Rich, moist soil in the coves and slopes supports the tall hardwood forest.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, logs and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
